details:
**Retrieving bones from Mictlan to create humanity**
At the start of the Fifth Sun (the current world age), Quetzalcoatl traveled to Mictlan, the Aztec underworld, to retrieve the bones of the people of the previous age from the death god Mictlantecuhtli. After returning, the bones were ground into a flour by the goddess Cihuacoatl ("Snake Woman"), and Quetzalcoatl sprinkled them with his own blood, drawn from his penis, to create the humans of the fifth world.

**The conch shell with no holes**
To test Quetzalcoatl, Mictlantecuhtli demanded that he blow a conch shell trumpet that had no holes. Quetzalcoatl had worms bore holes in it and bees fly inside to make it sound. Mictlantecuhtli then had a pit dug for him; startled by quail, Quetzalcoatl fell in and the bones broke, explaining why people come in different sizes.

**Sleeping with his sister and self-immolation**
Tricked by his rival Tezcatlipoca, who showed him a distorted image of himself in a mirror and got him drunk on the alcoholic drink pulque, Quetzalcoatl broke his vow of celibacy by sleeping with his sister, a celibate priestess. In shame he lay in a stone chest or threw himself on a funeral pyre and burned himself, and his heart rose into the sky as the morning star, the planet Venus.

**Tezcatlipoca**
Quetzalcoatl's chief rival and sometimes brother, whose name means "Smoking Mirror." Tezcatlipoca lost a foot (replaced with an obsidian mirror) to the earth monster Cipactli, which the two gods helped kill to create the earth. In the cycle of world ages, the two repeatedly toppled each other's suns; Quetzalcoatl once struck Tezcatlipoca into the sea, where he became a jaguar. Quetzalcoatl is sometimes called the "White Tezcatlipoca."

**Xolotl**
Quetzalcoatl's dog-headed twin brother, a psychopomp god of fire, sickness, and the underworld, who accompanies him to Mictlan. Xolotl represents the evening star, complementing Quetzalcoatl as the morning star, so both are associated with Venus.

**Raft of snakes and Hernan Cortes**
In the legend of his exile from the city of Tollan, Quetzalcoatl sailed east on a raft of serpents, promising to return. Because he was sometimes described as light-skinned and bearded, a later legend claims that Moctezuma II mistook the Spanish conquistador Hernan Cortes for the returning god, easing the conquest of Tenochtitlan.

**Ehecatl**
Quetzalcoatl's aspect as the wind god, depicted wearing a conical hat and a mask with a duck-like beak through which he blows the wind. Ehecatl blew on the motionless sun and moon to set them moving, and was worshipped in round temples. He fell in love with the goddess Mayahuel, bringing love (and the maguey plant) into the world.

**Wind jewel**
A pendant cut from a cross-section of a conch shell, called the "spirally voluted wind jewel" (ehecailacacozcatl). Quetzalcoatl wears it as a symbol of the wind, and priests and rulers wore similar shell ornaments.

**Birth from Chimalman**
In one version of his birth, the virgin goddess Chimalman conceived Quetzalcoatl after swallowing an emerald (a precious green stone). In another, the hunting god Mixcoatl shot an arrow at Chimalman and fathered him. Other sources name Coatlicue or the dual creator Ometeotl as his parent.

**Humans turned into monkeys**
Quetzalcoatl ruled one of the earlier world ages, or Suns. That age ended when a great hurricane swept the world away and its people were turned into monkeys.

**Turning into an ant to find maize**
After a red ant revealed where it was getting maize, Quetzalcoatl turned himself into a black ant and followed it into the Mountain of Our Sustenance (Tonacatepetl). He carried the corn kernels back to give food to the newly created humans.

**One Reed**
Quetzalcoatl's calendar name, Ce Acatl ("One Reed"). The coincidence that Cortes arrived in a One Reed year (1519) fed the legend that he was the returning god.

**Tollan**
The legendary Toltec city (Tula) whose priest-king, Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, is often conflated with the god. He ruled as a wise, celibate king who opposed human sacrifice, until Tezcatlipoca tricked him into abdicating and leaving.

**Patron of priests, learning, and the calendar**
Quetzalcoatl was the patron of Aztec priests and was credited with inventing books and the calendar. A temple dedicated to him at Teotihuacan (the Temple of the Feathered Serpent) may have been used to track the 260-day ritual calendar, and the Great Pyramid of Cholula, the largest pyramid in the world by volume, was dedicated to him.

**Kukulcan**
The Maya equivalent of Quetzalcoatl, whose name likewise means "feathered serpent." He is most famously associated with El Castillo, the pyramid at Chichen Itza.
